newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to allow news groups to open in Cuba.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to allow news groups to open in Cuba.

text.p: The White House is set to announce on Wednesday that the United States will grant licenses to 10 organisations to open news-gathering offices in Cuba, U.S. administration sources told Reuters.

The sources said the Clinton administration would grant the licenses to television networks CNN, CBS and ABC, the Associated Press wire service, newspapers the Miami Herald, the Fort Lauderdale Sun-Sentinel and the Chicago Tribune, the news agency and newspaper group Dow Jones, and the Spanish-language television network Univision.
A license was also to go to CubaINFO, which is associated with the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies.
The organisations must now seek approval from the Cuban government to set up operations in Havana.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry was expected to announce the move later on Wednesday.

The decision reflects a U.S. desire to increase the flow of information from the United States to Cuba. The thinking is that objective news reports from Havana to the United States will be beamed back to Cuba and help convince Cubans of the benefits of democracy.

Sen. Jesse Helms, the North Carolina Republican who chairs the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, had urged Clinton to approve the applications. CNN had actively sought U.S. approval to open a bureau in Cuba.

President Bill Clinton announced in October 1995 that he would allow U.S. news organisations to open offices in Havana for the first time in more than three decades in an effort to promote direct contacts between the United States and the Cuban people.
About a dozen news organisations applied for licenses, but a formal decision was delayed by the February 1996 shooting down of two Florida-based civilian aircraft by the Cuban Airforce.
CNN had no immediate comment but broadcasting sources said the cable network had already been approved by the Cubans to set up a bureau.
An ABC source said: "We have received U.S. approval and now must approach the Cuban authorities."
The CBS bureau will be a combined operation of CBS and its Spanish-language unit TeleNoticias.
Earl Maucker, editor of the Sun-Sentinel in Fort Lauderdale, confirmed the newspaper had received U.S. permission for a Havana office and said it was negotiating with Cuban officials.
"We're prepared to move immediately and set up a news operation in Havana once we receive proper permission from the Cuban government," Maucker said.
